The Round-eared tube-nosed fruit bat Nyctimene cyclotis is a relatively small pteropodid endemic to the islands of New Guinea and surrounding archipelagos. Field studies indicate that adult females reach a maximum body mass of 40.4 grams [Wwi = 40.4 grams], a value that places this species among the smaller members of its genus. Newborn pups, based on allometric relationships derived from the congener Eonycteris spelaea, are estimated to weigh approximately 3.0 grams [Wwb = approximately 3.0 grams] at birth, reflecting the altricial state typical of many fruit bats. This modest neonatal mass necessitates an extended period of maternal investment before the young can achieve nutritional independence. The measured rate also reflects the energetic costs of maintaining homeothermy at the species' preferred thermal set point, which is typical of tropical mammals that rarely encounter environmental temperatures far below their thermoneutral zone. Such physiological data are crucial for parameterizing energetic models of population persistence, as they directly inform the daily energy requirements of individuals across different life stages. Understanding these requirements is particularly important when considering the constraints imposed by gestation and lactation on the energy budget of reproductive females.

During this extended juvenile phase, individuals learn to navigate their foraging environment and develop the social skills necessary for colonial roosting. The delay between weaning and the onset of gonadal activity also serves to avoid reproductive competition with older, more experienced adults. Achieving this developmental milestone marks the transition to a reproductively viable adult, capable of contributing to the next generation.

Paleontological and comparative life-history data indicate that Nyctimene cyclotis occupies a slow end of the fast-slow continuum among small mammals. The maximum documented lifespan of 10.1 years [am = 10.1 years] is notably high for an animal with a female asymptotic mass of only 40.4 grams [Wwi = 40.4 grams], consistent with the demographic patterns observed in other island-dwelling pteropodids that face few terrestrial predators at a temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. The slow life history of N. cyclotis, with delayed reproduction and modest annual reproductive output, makes the species particularly vulnerable to environmental perturbation.
